summary.text: The asserted additive recurrence, compared with the defining gcd recurrence, forces all subsequent consecutive terms to be coprime. But a Fibonacci-matrix computation modulo \(195318521017\), using the finitely computed values at indices \(3773,3774\), shows that the consecutive terms at indices \(249580077006\) and \(249580077007\) are both divisible by this modulus, a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\geq 1}\) be the sequence defined by
\[
a_1=a_2=1,
\qquad
a_n=g_n+\frac{a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}}{g_n}\quad(n\geq3),
\qquad
g_n=\gcd(a_{n-1},a_{n-2}).
\]
We prove that the asserted collection of identities cannot hold for every \(n\geq3775\). In fact, only the first asserted identity,
\[
a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2},                                      \tag{1}
\]
is needed for the contradiction.

First note that every \(a_n\) is positive. This is immediate for \(a_1,a_2\). Inductively, if the preceding terms are positive, their gcd is positive, and the expression defining the next term is therefore positive.

We will use the following elementary observation. Suppose \(x,y\) are positive integers, put
\[
g=\gcd(x,y),\qquad S=x+y,
\]
and suppose
\[
g+\frac{S}{g}=1+S.                                         \tag{2}
\]
Then \(g=1\). Indeed, \(g\mid x\) and \(g\mid y\), so \(g\mid S\); write \(S=gq\). Equation (2) becomes
\[
g+q=1+gq,
\]
or equivalently
\[
(g-1)(q-1)=0.
\]
If \(g\ne1\), this forces \(q=1\), and hence \(S=g\). But \(g\leq x<x+y=S\), since \(y>0\), which is impossible. Thus \(g=1\), as claimed.

Now assume, for contradiction, the entire OEIS conjecture. In particular, assume (1) for every \(n\geq3775\). For every integer \(m\geq1\), apply the defining recurrence and (1) at the index \(3774+m\). If
\[
x=a_{3773+m},\qquad y=a_{3772+m},\qquad g=\gcd(x,y),
\]
then the defining recurrence says
\[
a_{3774+m}=g+\frac{x+y}{g},
\]
whereas (1) says
\[
a_{3774+m}=1+x+y.
\]
The preceding observation therefore gives
\[
\gcd(a_{3773+m},a_{3772+m})=1\qquad(m\geq1).                 \tag{3}
\]
Thus the conjecture would force every adjacent pair beginning with \((a_{3773},a_{3774})\) to be coprime.

Next shift the terms by one. Define
\[
b_m=a_{3773+m}+1\qquad(m\geq0).
\]
For every \(m\geq0\), identity (1), used at \(n=3775+m\), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{m+2}
 &=a_{3775+m}+1\\
 &=\bigl(1+a_{3774+m}+a_{3773+m}\bigr)+1\\
 &=(a_{3774+m}+1)+(a_{3773+m}+1)\\
 &=b_{m+1}+b_m.
\end{aligned}                                                \tag{4}
\]
Consequently, under the conjecture, the sequence \((b_m)\) is a Fibonacci-type sequence with initial values
\[
b_0=a_{3773}+1,\qquad b_1=a_{3774}+1.
\]

We now carry out a finite modular computation. Set
\[
p=195318521017
\]
and work modulo \(p\). No primality property of \(p\) is needed; only \(p>1\) will matter at the end.

The initial residues are obtained by direct iteration of the original defining recurrence from \((a_1,a_2)=(1,1)\) through index \(3774\). More explicitly, starting with the ordered pair \((x,y)=(1,1)\), repeatedly replace it by
\[
\left(y,\;\gcd(x,y)+\frac{x+y}{\gcd(x,y)}\right).
\]
After \(3772\) such replacements the pair is \((a_{3773},a_{3774})\). At every step the gcd is found by the Euclidean algorithm and the displayed division is exact. Reducing the final pair modulo \(p\) gives
\[
a_{3773}\equiv77940394258\pmod p,
\qquad
a_{3774}\equiv99768150821\pmod p.
\]
Thus
\[
b_0\equiv77940394259\pmod p,
\qquad
b_1\equiv99768150822\pmod p.                                \tag{5}
\]
This calculation uses the original recurrence itself, not the conjectured eventual recurrence.

To propagate (5) efficiently over a large number of steps, let
\[
Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Equation (4) is equivalent to
\[
\binom{b_m}{b_{m+1}}=Q^m\binom{b_0}{b_1}.                   \tag{6}
\]
Indeed, multiplication by \(Q\) sends \((u,v)^T\) to \((v,u+v)^T\), exactly one step of the recurrence.

Take
\[
N=249580073233.
\]
Repeated squaring modulo \(p\) gives
\[
Q^N\equiv
\begin{pmatrix}
117378126758&21827756563\\
21827756563&139205883321
\end{pmatrix}\pmod p.                                      \tag{7}
\]
For completeness, this is a standard binary exponentiation using
\[
\begin{aligned}
N={}&2^{37}+2^{36}+2^{35}+2^{33}+2^{28}+2^{27}+2^{26}
      +2^{21}+2^{16}+2^{15}\\
   &\quad+2^{13}+2^{12}+2^8+2^4+2^0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Starting with \(Q\), one successively squares modulo \(p\) to obtain \(Q^{2^j}\), and multiplies precisely the matrices corresponding to these fifteen nonzero binary digits. The resulting matrix is the one displayed in (7). Equivalently, using the familiar identity
\[
Q^N=\begin{pmatrix}F_{N-1}&F_N\\F_N&F_{N+1}\end{pmatrix},
\]
the three entries computed modulo \(p\) are
\[
F_{N-1}\equiv117378126758,
\quad F_N\equiv21827756563,
\quad F_{N+1}\equiv139205883321.
\]

Multiplying the matrix in (7) by the initial vector in (5) produces \((1,1)^T\) modulo \(p\). The two scalar calculations are
\[
\begin{aligned}
&117378126758\cdot77940394259
 +21827756563\cdot99768150822\\
&\hspace{35mm}=57988419771\,p+1,
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
&21827756563\cdot77940394259
 +139205883321\cdot99768150822\\
&\hspace{35mm}=79816176334\,p+1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore (6) implies
\[
b_N\equiv1\pmod p,
\qquad b_{N+1}\equiv1\pmod p.                              \tag{8}
\]
Recalling that \(b_m=a_{3773+m}+1\), congruences (8) say
\[
a_{3773+N}\equiv0\pmod p,
\qquad
a_{3774+N}\equiv0\pmod p.                              \tag{9}
\]
In ordinary indices these are the consecutive terms
\[
a_{249580077006}\quad\text{and}\quad a_{249580077007}.
\]
Thus \(p\) divides both of them, and hence
\[
p\mid\gcd(a_{3774+N},a_{3773+N}).                          \tag{10}
\]

On the other hand, take \(m=N+1=249580073234\) in (3). Since
\[
3773+(N+1)=3774+N,
\qquad
3772+(N+1)=3773+N,
\]
formula (3) gives
\[
\gcd(a_{3774+N},a_{3773+N})=1.                              \tag{11}
\]
Combining (10) and (11) says that \(p\mid1\), which is impossible because
\[
p=195318521017>1.
\]

This contradiction arose solely from assuming that the first proposed identity holds for every \(n\geq3775\). Therefore that universal identity is false. A fortiori, it is false that for every \(n\geq3775\) all three proposed identities—including the second-difference identity and the explicit Fibonacci formula—hold simultaneously. This disproves the stated conjecture.
